full1_p1: Hobbits are not naturally a battle people. That is what makes them so interesting in play. Their strength is not in heavy armour, big shields and a thunderous charge, but in togetherness, courage out of necessity, supplies, news, light movement, common sense and the ability to survive even where larger nations find their pride too cramped.
full1_p2: For game purposes hobbits can be approached as a supporting, light and community-minded army of the Free Peoples. They can be messengers, cooks, quartermasters, scouts, water-bearers, careful archers, keepers of camp comfort, gatherers of news and small fighters who got into the battle mostly because someone had to hold the last way home.
full1_p3: A hobbit costume should look different from a human one at first sight. You don’t need to be physically small. What matters are proportions, layering, softness, country cut, colour, roundness and small civilian details: vest, shirt, breeches, braces, pockets, mug, unlit pipe, snack, map, lantern, tobacco pouch or a dried apple.
full2_p1: Hobbits are a small folk related to humans, known above all from the Shire, Rhovanion and around Bree. They tend to be smaller, with hairy feet that have hard skin, often walking barefoot, and curly hair. They aren’t a great historical nation of kings and wars, yet their unobtrusiveness has proven an unexpected strength in Middle-earth’s history.
full2_p2: Most hobbits prefer food, gardens, crafts, inns, songs, birthdays, gift-giving and a comfortable home over adventure. That doesn’t mean they are cowards. They are cautious, practical, and slow to believe that the great events of history really concern their fields and pantries.
full2_p3: For play purposes you can distinguish hobbits from the quieter Shire, the bolder Brandybucks and Tooks, the more water-loving Stoors and the more practical hobbits from Bree. You don’t have to copy the exact family lineage. It’s enough that the costume and behaviour show a small country folk who view war with mistrust but won’t let their friends down.
full3_p1: Hobbit clothing is based on comfortable country wear. Linen or cotton shirts, wool vests, knee breeches, braces, wide belts, colourful scarves, soft jackets, capes, hoods and simple caps all fit. Colours can be earthy, but hobbits can carry more colour than soldiers: green, brown, beige, yellow, burgundy, dark blue and muted red.
full3_p2: The most important thing is not to look modern. A T-shirt, hoodie, sports trousers and trainers without cover destroy a hobbit instantly. Modern boots can be hidden under foot covers, leg wraps or fur covers to give the impression of hobbit feet. Walking barefoot in the terrain is not recommended for safety reasons.
full3_p3: Small props belong to a hobbit. A wooden spoon, mug, napkin, small pan, basket, food pouch, lantern, recipe book, map, letter, ball of string or a small spade do more than re-equipping into heavy armour. A hobbit should look like they originally went out to run an errand and somebody dragged them into history by mistake.
full4_p1: A hobbit is, above all, not a heavy infantryman. If they fight, a short sword, a dagger according to the rules, a staff, a small round shield, a sling-stylisation per rules, a light bow or a simple spear all suit. Equipment should be small, practical and rather defensive. Heavy two-handed weapons and large metal armour usually don’t fit a hobbit.
full4_p2: A camp-support role works very well. Hobbits can help with water, food, small tasks, messages, escorting newcomers, trade, coins, watches and the in-camp atmosphere. If they take part in battle, they can hold the second line, protect the banner, escort the wounded, carry messages or support the bigger fighters.
full4_p3: A hobbit group should play on togetherness. An individual can be comic, but a group of hobbits should be a small island of home in the middle of war. A shared breakfast, regular snacks, “fundamental” debates about pies and a calm resistance to grand speeches can be a very strong part of the atmosphere.
full5_p1: Hobbits don’t usually come to the event to win the contest for the most fearsome look. Their tone is friendly, nosy, a little careful and a little cheeky. They might ask why everyone looks so serious, whether lunch is coming yet and whether it’s really necessary to go to battle right now.
full5_p2: A nice contrast works well: a hobbit is afraid, but goes anyway. Doesn’t want to be a hero, but does the right thing. Doesn’t want to leave camp, but if a friend goes, goes with them. Doesn’t know grand strategy, but knows exactly where the water is, who has the last bandage and who lost their mug.
full5_p3: For newcomers, a hobbit is a very pleasant role. The costume can start simple and grow. You don’t need expensive armour. The key is a comfortable country look, modern items covered up, and the willingness to play small situations with others.
full6_l1: A shirt, vest, breeches, braces and a cloak make a base in one evening.
full6_l2: Use earthy and gently cheerful colours: green, brown, beige, yellow, burgundy.
full6_l3: Cover modern boots with foot covers, fur or leg wraps. Don’t walk barefoot in dangerous terrain.
full6_l4: Add civilian props: mug, spoon, basket, map, lantern, snack.
full6_l5: Keep weapons small and practical. A hobbit should look clever, not like a knight at half size.
full6_l6: In a group, agree on a family or village element: scarves, buttons, a patch, vest colour or a round-door symbol.
